title: User-Driven Comments on a Facebook Advertisement Recruiting Canadian Parents in a Study on Immunization: Content Analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of all 117 user comments posted on 2 Facebook recruitment advertisements. Two raters coded every claim against the WHO SAGE Working Group vaccine-hesitancy matrix, and the paper reports a quantitative share of claims coded as displaying lack of knowledge/awareness on immunization 'including misinformation' (27/130, 20.8%), with an explicit accuracy sub-split (22/27, 81% providing inaccurate information or misperceptions). That is a share of items judged against an accuracy standard with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. Sentiment codes (positive/negative/hesitant/ambiguous) are NOT extracted: anti-vaccination sentiment is not a veracity judgement.

estimates.measure_type: % of claims in the non-positive comments coded as lack of knowledge or awareness on immunization (misinformation plus belief in own research/knowledge)
estimates.denominator: 130 claims made in the 66 negative, hesitant or ambiguous comments posted in the Comments section of 2 Facebook advertisements targeting Canadian parents
estimates.definition: A claim was counted if the two raters coded it under the WHO SAGE WG theme 'Lack of knowledge or awareness', defined in Table 1 as 'misinformation and belief in own knowledge or research' — e.g. courts admitted vaccines cause autism, vaccines cause decreased brain function, vaccinated children lack basic immunity.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition; the coded category is "Lack of knowledge or awareness (misinformation and belief in own knowledge or research)", and the Discussion states "information in the negative comments was often inaccurate and the risks of immunization were misperceived".
estimates.source_quote:
Inaccurate knowledge (27/130, 20.8%) and misperceptions of risk (23/130, 17.7%) were most prevalent
     in the 130 nonpositive comments.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Themes in the Negative, Hesitant, and Ambiguous Comments' (p. 5) and Table 1 (p. 6)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 2 raters (JLT and BL) independently coded every comment and claim in NVivo 10 against the WHO SAGE Working Group vaccine-hesitancy matrix; 'The 2 raters independently categorized all comments (negative and positive) and claims within the comments, and achieved over 95% consensus', remaining items discussed to 100% consensus; a third rater was available but the framework was pre-established.
estimates.moderator_quote: In the 66 negative, hesitant, or ambiguous comments, 130 claims were made on factors affecting vaccination decisions.
estimates.notes: Borderline for two reasons an adjudicator should see. (1) The denominator is CLAIMS (130) drawn only from the 66 negative/hesitant/ambiguous comments — not from all 117 comments and not from all 204 claims — so it is a curated, non-positive subset, and the % is not a prevalence over everything a Facebook user would have seen. (2) The numerator category bundles genuine misinformation with 'belief in own knowledge or research', which is not itself a false statement; breadth is therefore coded at the loosest level (misleading). The purer accuracy figure is the 22/27 sub-split carried in the next row. Data collection ran 12 Dec 2013 - 11 Jan 2014; year coded 2013 as the midpoint of that window falls in December 2013.

estimates.measure_type: % of the 'lack of knowledge or awareness' claims that provided inaccurate information or misperceptions on immunization
estimates.denominator: 27 claims already coded as displaying lack of knowledge or awareness on immunization
estimates.definition: Within the 27 'lack of knowledge' claims, the share whose content was inaccurate information or a misperception about immunization, as opposed to a claim asserting the credibility of one's own research.
estimates.misinfo_def: "providing inaccurate information or misperceptions on immunization"
estimates.source_quote: knowledge), with the majority (22/27, 81%) providing inaccurate
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Themes in the Negative, Hesitant, and Ambiguous Comments' (p. 5)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-rater NVivo coding against the WHO SAGE WG matrix, over 95% consensus then 100% after discussion; accuracy judged by the raters, no external fact-check source named.
estimates.moderator_quote: Within this theme, 20.8% (27/130) of the claims displayed lack of knowledge or awareness on immunization (including misinformation and the belief in their own research and knowledge)
estimates.notes: R3 row: falsity measured INSIDE an already-misinformation-flagged set (the 27 lack-of-knowledge claims), so within_misinfo_content=true and it belongs in the appendix, not in prevalence pooling. Verbatim numerator and denominator.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Sentiment shares are reported for all 117 comments — positive 51/117 (43.6%), negative 41/117 (35.0%), ambiguous 20/117 (17.1%), hesitant 5/117 (4.3%). NOT extracted: negative/anti-vaccination sentiment is not a veracity judgement, and a wholly accurate comment could be coded negative. 2) Link trustworthiness: '11.9% (14/117) posted links to websites. Of the 14 website links, 2 were from trustworthy sources'. The implied 12/14 non-trustworthy is a complement I would have to compute, barred by R8, so no row. 3) I did not create a 22/130 (16.9%) row for 'inaccurate claims as a share of all non-positive claims'; both counts are verbatim, but it stitches two separately reported ratios and the paper never states it, so I kept the two ratios as the paper reports them. 4) Other Table 1/Table 2 theme shares (mistrust in pharma 18/130, risk perception 23/130, positive-claim themes 29/74 etc.) are attitude/argument themes, not falsity codes. 5) '28% of adults reported to believe that there is or be uncertain about a link between vaccines and autism' is cited from reference [43] (Greenberg et al), not this study's data, and belief is excluded anyway. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a -layout rendering of a two-column print page, so the printed sentence is interleaved with the neighbouring column and is not contiguous in the file; row 1's source_quote is therefore the exact within-line column fragment carrying the 81% value (the sentence continues 'information or misperceptions on immunization ... (5/27, 19%)'). Row 0's quote is taken from the full-width abstract, where the same 27/130, 20.8% figure is stated contiguously.

rob.design: Content analysis of a full census of user comments (117 comments by 85 unique users, after excluding 9 off-topic comments) spontaneously posted on 2 Facebook recruitment advertisements shown to Canadian parents, 12 Dec 2013 - 11 Jan 2014; no sampling and no response rate (unsolicited commenters, self-selected). Two raters independently coded type of comment, sex, main message and claims, using the WHO SAGE WG matrix for non-positive claims and an inductively derived scheme for positive claims; reliability reported only as 'over 95% consensus' rising to 100% after discussion — no kappa. Authors note commenter count may be overestimated (multiple accounts unverifiable) and that results are not generalizable.
rob.item6_quote: We categorized claims about vaccination within the comments according to the major themes and subthemes; claims could be classified into one or more themes and subcategories within the themes.
rob.item10_quote: In the 66 negative, hesitant, or ambiguous comments, 130 claims were made on factors affecting vaccination decisions. Individual and social group influence was the predominant theme in the claims within the posted comments (85/130, 65.4%). Within this theme, 20.8% (27/130) of the claims displayed lack of knowledge or awareness on immunization (including misinformation and the belief in their own research and knowledge)
